claims.text: Rapid quenching of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 by melt spinning at 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous structure.
The rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 amorphous structure is a high-energy structure.
The rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 structure contains substantial residual stress.
A short annealing hold at Tg minus 5–10 K can relax amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 without inducing crystallization.
Applying the sub-Tg anneal immediately after quenching is important to the proposed benefit.
Sub-Tg annealing reduces free volume in the amorphous matrix.
Sub-Tg annealing relaxes residual stresses in the amorphous matrix.
Sub-Tg annealing permits local atomic rearrangement into a lower-energy glass configuration.
The lower-energy relaxed configuration reduces the thermodynamic driving force for crystallization.
Structural relaxation will mitigate unpredictable phase transformations during subsequent reheating.
Sub-Tg-annealed Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than an untreated rapidly quenched control.
Sub-Tg-annealed samples will exhibit diminished crystallization exotherms during reheating.
Sub-Tg annealing will improve retention of the amorphous phase during subsequent thermal exposure.
The unannealed Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy has limited amorphous retention following rapid quenching.
The unannealed alloy has a complicated thermal response during solidification and reheating.
The intervention should succeed only under cooling conditions sufficiently rapid to first form an amorphous state, such as 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Annealing too close to the crystallization regime or for too long may negate relaxation benefits or induce crystallization.
DSC, XRD, and TEM can compare crystallization behavior and amorphous retention between annealed and unannealed Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 samples.
